extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, undergraduate discrete/combinatorics instructors, and researchers studying proof schemes and student reasoning about proof
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Harel & Sowder’s proof-schemes framework and Lockwood’s model of combinatorial thinking to analyze how undergraduate students produce and characterize combinatorial proofs of binomial identities. Focus is on students' justificatory schemes (e.g., ritual, authoritarian, analytical) and on components needed for valid combinatorial proofs (sets, counting processes, expressions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial proof (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A combinatorial proof argues for an identity by arguing that each side enumerates a (finite) set of outcomes; the validity lies in the fact that a set can have only one cardinality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Pascal’s identity proved by counting committees of size k from n people—both sides count the same set. Combinatorial proofs typically verbally unpack symbols rather than manipulate them algebraically; they may be bijective (construct a bijection between sets) or use case breakdowns/counting processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylianides' classroom-community proof acceptance criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof is a connected sequence of assertions against a mathematical claim that: (1) uses statements accepted by the classroom community that are true and available without further justification; (2) employs forms of reasoning that are valid and within the conceptual reach of the classroom community; (3) is communicated with modes of expression appropriate and within the conceptual reach of the classroom community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broader notion of proof is used in the study to decide what counts as a proof for the participants’ communities; it emphasizes social/communicative acceptability in addition to deductive validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: External conviction proof schemes (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: A class of proof schemes where doubts are removed by ritualistic characteristics of an argument, the word of an authority, or the symbolic form of an argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harel & Sowder organize external conviction into ritual, authoritarian, and symbolic sub-schemes; these are considered less sophisticated and may lead students to accept or reject combinatorial proofs for non-mathematical reasons (appearance, authority, or presence/absence of symbols).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are convinced by the appearance of an argument rather than its correctness—e.g., saying 'it just looks like a proof'—or they doubt proofs that lack familiar symbolic expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ritual schemes can cause students to reject combinatorial proofs because such proofs often consist only of words and lack symbolic manipulation; conversely, ritual acceptance can make students accept nonrigorous arguments that merely look like proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritarian proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Students accept a statement as true based solely on the word of an authority (teacher, textbook) rather than on intrinsic justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May manifest as accepting a combinatorial proof because 'the teacher presented it on the board' without understanding why it is valid; instructors should be wary of students relying on authority rather than understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Students conceive of proof primarily as symbolic manipulation and may not regard arguments that lack symbolic computations as valid proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because combinatorial proofs often do not employ algebraic manipulation, students holding symbolic schemes may be less likely to accept combinatorial proofs as rigorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical proof schemes (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof schemes that fall short of deductive reasoning and rely on empirical checks or perceptual/visual impressions; Harel & Sowder list inductive and perceptual subtypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical schemes can include checking specific cases (inductive) or relying on mental images/intuition (perceptual); the authors note these are generally less robust than analytical schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Conviction by quantitatively evaluating a statement for one or more specific cases (checking examples) rather than deriving a general deductive proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors did not expect this to feature heavily because participants produced general enumerative arguments, but it is a recognized way students might be convinced (e.g., checking n=3 for a binomial identity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptual proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Conviction through perceptual observations or rudimentary mental images that lack the ability to transform or anticipate transformations (e.g., sketching examples to feel convinced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although often visual (geometry), a perceptual scheme might manifest for combinatorial proofs as accepting them as 'intuitive justifications' rather than full analytical proofs; the paper hypothesizes this could make combinatorial proofs feel less rigorous to students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical proof schemes (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof schemes that validate conjectures by means of logical deductions and are generally accepted as rigorous mathematical proofs; broken into transformational and axiomatic classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical schemes are the most sophisticated in Harel & Sowder’s hierarchy; recognizing combinatorial proofs as analytically valid is a key outcome the study investigates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformational proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Students perform meaningful, goal-oriented operations on mathematical objects and anticipate the results, using meanings and relationships among objects to make deductions leading to a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In combinatorial proofs, transformational schemes correspond to interpreting expressions as counting sets and performing operations (case breakdowns, enumeration) that logically lead to equality of cardinalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformational — contextual restrictive
rubrics_metrics.description: A transformational scheme that is restricted to a particular context (e.g., proving an identity only within the context of committees rather than generally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students may accept a combinatorial proof only as valid in the restrictive context described (committees), failing to see that the argument generalizes because a set has one cardinality; instructors should address the generality of combinatorial arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformational — generic proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Students interpret a statement generally but can only express the proof in a particular numerical case (use a specific example to stand for the general argument).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While no instance was observed in the study, the authors note it as a possible restrictive transformational scheme relevant to combinatorial reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformational — constructive proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: A restrictive transformational stance where students believe existence proofs must be constructive; they may reject nonconstructive proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors consider this unlikely to appear in combinatorial proof contexts, but it is listed among transformational variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic proof scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Students understand that mathematical justification can be grounded in undefined terms and axioms (proofs starting in principle from axioms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper does not expand on this scheme because participants did not refer to axioms in their activity, but it remains part of Harel & Sowder’s analytical category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lockwood’s model — sets of outcomes (component)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three components of combinatorial thinking: collections of objects being enumerated (how outcomes are represented or encoded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizing the target set that expressions enumerate is central to constructing a combinatorial proof (e.g., committees, binary strings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lockwood’s model — counting processes (component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental or procedural operations used to generate the set of outcomes (e.g., multiplication principle, case breakdowns, selecting elements in stages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressions often suggest counting processes (e.g., addition suggests case breakdown); combinatorial proofs explicitly describe or map a counting process to an expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lockwood’s model — formulas/expressions (component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical expressions whose numerical values are the cardinality of the enumerated set (the algebraic side of the identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreting these expressions as counts of particular processes is necessary for a combinatorial proof (e.g., n−1 choose k−1 suggests picking one object then k−1 from remaining).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mappings between expressions, processes, and sets
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid combinatorial proof demonstrates coherent mappings: expressions ↔ counting processes ↔ sets of outcomes, showing both sides count the same set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mapping is central: expressions should suggest underlying processes, processes generate outcome sets, and one must argue both sides enumerate the same set (or produce a bijection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijective combinatorial proofs (variant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinatorial proofs that argue each side counts different sets and then construct a bijection between these sets (bijective proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper notes bijective proofs exist but states they do not focus on them; they are an alternative valid combinatorial proof style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for explanatory/convincing arguments (Lockwood et al., 2020)
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument is explanatory to an individual within a representation system if it: (1) begins with axioms, definitions, or statements the individual believes are true; (2) employs inferential schemes that are natural; (3) is couched within, or can be mapped to, a representation system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a lens to judge whether combinatorial proofs are explanatory/convincing to students; emphasizes representation-system fit and naturalness of inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features of combinatorial proofs that affect student acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinatorial proofs are often exclusively verbal (sentences and paragraphs), are context-specific (committees, lattice paths, binary strings), and typically lack symbolic algebraic manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features can make combinatorial proofs feel less rigorous to students who expect symbolic manipulation or who adhere to 'examples aren’t proofs'; instructors should explicitly clarify why correct combinatorial proofs are rigorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common student difficulties and anti-patterns in combinatorial proof reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed or documented issues include pseudo-semantic proof production (relying on syntax of prior proofs without semantic understanding), treating examples as general proofs, restricting proofs to specific contexts, failing to map expressions to counting processes, and equating absence of symbols with lack of rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior studies (Engelke & CadwalladerOlsker; others) categorized such difficulties and suggested scaffolds (e.g., prompting 'How many…?' questions) to help students produce correct combinatorial proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of case breakdowns and multiplication principle as validity moves
rubrics_metrics.description: Valid combinatorial proofs use case breakdowns (addition) or staged counting/Multiplication Principle (product) to enumerate disjoint subsets or sequential choices that together count the target set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Pascal’s identity uses a case breakdown excluding/including a particular person; the Multiplication Principle is formalized and should be applied carefully (independence of stages, distinct composite outcomes).
